lessons.title: Ziffer plus zehn — the rule
lessons.gloss: the rule that makes every teen — a digit you own, with zehn welded on the end

segments.text: The leftover trick covered two numbers and stopped. From here German uses one rule, and it does not break once.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a digit, then zehn

segments.text: Take a digit you already own. Put zehn on the end. That is the number.

utterances: take a digit: drei. weld on: zehn. and say it: —.

segments.text: No space, no linking piece, no change to either half. Say that row out loud and you have made the number yourself; the next lesson only confirms it.
You are not learning eight new words in this chapter — you are running one machine eight times.
English does the identical thing and hides it slightly: -teen is ten. Thir-teen is "three-ten," which is why it rhymes with nothing and means exactly what German means.
z-ts — every one of these ends in zehn, and German z is ts, so every one ends -TSAYN.
Say zehn on its own until the ts is automatic. It is about to appear eight times in a row.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the rule — "a digit, then zehn"]

segments.instruction: run it once — "drei", then "zehn", then the two joined
segments.source: [YOU SAY: run it once — "drei", then "zehn", then the two joined]
[YOU SAY: what English hides — "-teen is ten"]

segments.text: "Ziffer plus zehn."

What is the rule? (A digit, then zehn.) Does anything go between them? (No.) Run it on drei and say what comes out. How does every one of them end? (-tsayn.) And what is English -teen? (Ten.) Next: the rule's first run.

lessons.title: dreizehn — "thirteen"
lessons.gloss: thirteen — the rule's first run, and it is exactly what you would predict

segments.text: You have the rule and you have the digit. Say the number before you read it.
dreizehn — "thirteen." drei + zehn.
Nothing added, nothing changed. If you predicted it, that is the point of the chapter working.
English wore its digit down — three became thir- — and German did not touch its own.
diphthong-ei — ei is the vowel of English eye, unchanged from drei.
z-ts — and the second half is -TSAYN.
DREI-tsayn, with the weight on the digit, not the ending. That stress pattern holds for every number in this chapter.

segments.instruction: the English one and its worn-down digit — "thirteen, from three"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the English one and its worn-down digit — "thirteen, from three"]

segments.text: "drei, zehn, dreizehn."
Say "thirteen." (Dreizehn.) What are its halves? (Drei and zehn.) Did either change? (No.) Which syllable is stressed? (The first — the digit.) Next: fourteen, the same way.

lessons.title: vierzehn — "fourteen"
lessons.gloss: fourteen — the rule's second run, with the V that is an f

segments.text: Same rule, next digit — and its first letter is one you have been warned about twice.
vierzehn — "fourteen." vier + zehn.
v-as-f — the V is an f, exactly as in vier and Vater.
z-ts — and -TSAYN again.
FEER-tsayn. Third time for that v: a number, a father, and now a teen.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two so far — "dreizehn, vierzehn"]

segments.text: "dreizehn, vierzehn."
Say "fourteen." (Vierzehn.) How is the V said? (As an f.) What are its halves? (Vier and zehn.) Next: fifteen.

lessons.title: fünfzehn — "fifteen"
lessons.gloss: fifteen — the rule's third run, and where English clipped and German did not

segments.text: Third run of the rule, and the first place English is the messier of the two languages.
fünfzehn — "fifteen." fünf + zehn.
The digit is whole. English is not: five became fif-, so fifteen no longer shows its own number. German keeps fünf visible and audible.
umlaut-ue — the ü from fünf, unchanged: say ee, then round the lips.
z-ts — and -TSAYN.
Two syllables, the weight on fünf and the ending unstressed.

segments.instruction: three in a row — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: three in a row — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn"]
[YOU SAY: what English lost — "five became fif-"]

segments.text: "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn."
Say "fifteen." (Fünfzehn.) Is the digit whole? (Yes.) Is English's? (No — five became fif-.) Say the three you have. (Dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn.) Next: where German clips too.

lessons.title: The two clipped digits
lessons.gloss: the two places German shortens a digit before zehn, and it is for the mouth, not for the grammar

segments.text: The rule holds for every number in this chapter. Two of them shorten the digit first, and it is worth knowing which before you meet them.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two digits get shortened

utterances: the digit: sechs. before zehn it becomes: sech-. why: the s would collide with the ts of zehn.
the digit: sieben. before zehn it becomes: sieb-. why: the -en is an unstressed syllable too many.

segments.text: Both are the mouth economising, not the grammar changing. It is still a digit with zehn on the end; the digit has been worn smooth at the join and nothing more.
English did the same thing and did more of it. Three became thir- and five became fif-, and nobody thinks of thirteen as irregular — it is a worn compound, exactly like these two.

So the honest scoreboard is: English clips two digits, German clips two digits, and they are not the same two. German keeps fünf whole where English does not; English keeps six and seven whole where German does not. Neither language is tidier. Both are old, and old words get worn.

segments.instruction: what English clipped instead — "three to thir-, five to fif-"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what English clipped instead — "three to thir-, five to fif-"]

segments.instruction: what has not changed — "still a digit, then zehn"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what has not changed — "still a digit, then zehn"]

segments.text: "sechs to sech-, sieben to sieb-."

Which two German digits shorten? (Sechs and sieben.) What do they become? (Sech- and sieb-.) Is the rule broken? (No — the digit is worn, the rule holds.) Which two did English clip? (Three and five.) Next: the first of the two.

lessons.title: sechzehn — "sixteen"
lessons.gloss: sixteen — sechs without its s, because the s and the ts would collide

segments.text: First of the two clipped ones. You already know what it drops.
sechzehn — "sixteen." sech- + zehn, with the s of sechs gone.
Try it with the s left in and you will hear the problem: sechs-zehn puts an s immediately before a ts, and the two will not sit next to each other.
ch-ach — the ch is the raspy one from acht and Nacht, made at the back.
z-ts — and then straight into -TSAYN.
ZECH-tsayn, where the first sound is the buzzed German s.

segments.instruction: four in a row — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: four in a row — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn"]

segments.text: "sechs, sechzehn."
Say "sixteen." (Sechzehn.) What did the digit lose? (Its s.) Why? (It would collide with the ts.) Is the rule still digit + zehn? (Yes.) Next: the other clipped one.

lessons.title: siebzehn — "seventeen"
lessons.gloss: seventeen — sieben without its -en, one syllable saved

segments.text: Second and last of the clipped ones. After this the rule runs clean to twenty.
siebzehn — "seventeen." sieb- + zehn, with the -en of sieben gone.
Sieben-zehn would be four syllables for one number, three of them unstressed. German trimmed the middle and kept the meaning.
ie-long-ee — ie is a long ee, as in sieben.
consonant-b-final — the b stays a b here, because it is not really at the end of a word: zehn is welded on behind it.
z-ts — and -TSAYN.
ZEEB-tsayn.

segments.instruction: the two clipped ones together — "sechzehn, siebzehn"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two clipped ones together — "sechzehn, siebzehn"]

segments.text: "sieben, siebzehn."
Say "seventeen." (Siebzehn.) What did the digit lose? (Its -en.) Name both clipped numbers. (Sechzehn, siebzehn.) How many are left to clip? (None.) Next: eighteen, whole again.

lessons.title: achtzehn — "eighteen"
lessons.gloss: eighteen — the digit whole again, and the -cht you have had since Nacht

segments.text: The clipping is over. From here the digits go in whole.
achtzehn — "eighteen." acht + zehn, both whole.
ch-ach — the raspy ch of acht, unchanged.
z-ts — and -TSAYN.
That -cht is the one you were given twice: acht against English eight, Nacht against night. Where German rasps, English writes -ght and says nothing at all.

segments.instruction: the pair that shares the rasp — "acht, Nacht"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair that shares the rasp — "acht, Nacht"]
[YOU SAY: their silent English twins — "eight, night"]

segments.text: "acht, achtzehn."
Say "eighteen." (Achtzehn.) Was the digit clipped? (No — whole.) What does English write where German rasps? (-ght.) Next: nineteen.

lessons.title: neunzehn — "nineteen"
lessons.gloss: nineteen — the last of the -zehn numbers, and the rule's eighth clean run

segments.text: Eighth and last run of the rule. You should be able to say it before reading on.
neunzehn — "nineteen." neun + zehn, both whole.
Seven numbers built from one rule and not one of them broke it. Two shortened a digit at the join and kept the rule intact.
diphthong-eu — eu is the oy of English boy, unchanged from neun.
z-ts — and -TSAYN for the last time.
NOYN-tsayn.

segments.instruction: the last four — "sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the last four — "sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn"]

segments.text: "achtzehn, neunzehn."
Say "nineteen." (Neunzehn.) Its halves? (Neun and zehn.) How many numbers has the rule built? (Seven.) How many times did it break? (None.) Next: twenty, which stops using zehn.

lessons.title: zwanzig — "twenty"
lessons.gloss: twenty — where the ending changes from zehn to -zig

segments.text: Eight numbers ended in zehn. This one does not, and the ending it takes instead is worth a lesson of its own.
zwanzig — "twenty."
It opens like zwei and zwölf — tsv- — and then closes on -zig where every number before it closed on -zehn.
z-ts — twice: tsv- at the front, -ts- in the middle.
w-as-v — the w is a v, as always.
ich-laut — and the final -ig is said as the soft ich-sound from the very first chapters: -ikh, not -ig.
TSVAHN-tsikh. That final -ig rule holds for every German word ending the same way, so it is worth more than this one number.

segments.instruction: the three that open the same way — "zwei, zwölf, zwanzig"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three that open the same way — "zwei, zwölf, zwanzig"]

segments.text: "neunzehn, zwanzig."
Say "twenty." (Zwanzig.) How does the ending sound? (-ikh — the soft ich-sound.) Does it end in zehn? (No — -zig.) Which number is at the front? (Zwei.) Next: what -zig actually is.

lessons.title: -zig and -ty
lessons.gloss: twenty is two tens — and the -zig of German and the -ty of English are both ten, worn down

segments.text: The ending changed at twenty. It did not change subject.
Older Germanic twaintig, which is twain — "two" — plus tig, and tig is ten.

utterances: word: zwanzig. is: zwei + -zig. and means: two tens.
word: twenty. is: twain + -ty. and means: two tens.

segments.text: So -zig and -ty are the same ending, both of them ten worn down by being said a great many times. German's zehn stayed whole because it kept being used on its own; the version welded onto twenty wore out instead.
Stand back and the whole span from eleven to twenty is three ideas, and you have all three.
Eleven and twelve count what is left over after ten fingers.
Thirteen to nineteen are a digit with ten on the end.
Twenty is two tens, with the same ten worn to -zig.
Every one of those is a compound. Not one number in this chapter is a word you had to be given — they are all built, and the parts were yours before the chapter started.

segments.instruction: the two endings that are one word — "-zig, -ty, both ten"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two endings that are one word — "-zig, -ty, both ten"]

segments.text: "zwanzig — two tens."
What does zwanzig mean underneath? (Two tens.) What is -zig? (Ten, worn down.) And English -ty? (The same word.) So how many of this chapter's numbers are compounds? (All of them.)

lessons.title: Practice — thirteen to twenty
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — eight numbers from one rule, and a pattern that does not break where the Romance ones do

segments.text: No new words. One rule, run eight times, and two small wearings-down along the way.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the rule and its two exceptions that are not exceptions

segments.text: Six digits go in whole and two are trimmed at the join. The rule never changes.
Eleven to twenty is three ideas and you now hold all three: two leftovers, seven digit-plus-ten compounds, and one two-tens.

Here is the contrast worth carrying. The Romance sisters all break partway through the teens and switch to a different construction — Portuguese at sixteen, French and Italian at seventeen. German does not break at all. Two leftovers, then one clean rule to twenty, and English marches beside it the whole distance because it is doing the same thing with the same worn-down words.

segments.instruction: count from thirteen — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn, zwanzig"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: count from thirteen — "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn, zwanzig"]
[YOU SAY: the two trimmed digits — "sech-, sieb-"]

segments.instruction: the one that stops using zehn — "zwanzig"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the one that stops using zehn — "zwanzig"]

segments.instruction: count the whole span — "elf, zwölf, dreizehn … zwanzig"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: count the whole span — "elf, zwölf, dreizehn … zwanzig"]

segments.text: "dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn."

What is the rule from thirteen up? (A digit, then zehn.) Which two digits are trimmed? (Sechs and sieben.) Does the rule ever break? (No.) What is zwanzig underneath? (Two tens.) And where do the Romance languages break? (Partway through the teens — sixteen or seventeen.)
